analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 23.5% of firms in health care and social assistance reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 22.0% in the prior period, making this one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. The increment is modest but consistent, suggesting adoption is broadening steadily rather than spiking, and the base rate reflects a sector that spans large hospital systems alongside small social assistance providers with very different technology budgets and readiness.

The NIH frames the research infrastructure underlying much of clinical AI, working to make biomedical data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and explicitly aiming to make that data usable with AI and machine learning applications. NIH's data holdings span electronic health records, omics data, imaging data, and disease-specific repositories, and the agency identifies establishing coordinated partnerships to empower researchers across the United States as a core objective alongside setting policies and best practices for AI in biomedical and behavioral research. That federal infrastructure shapes what models get built and on what evidence base.

Measuring whether models are good enough for clinical settings has become a distinct problem, and OpenAI's HealthBench represents the most detailed public attempt to answer it. Built with 262 physicians who have practiced in 60 countries, HealthBench includes 5,000 realistic health conversations each graded against physician-written rubric criteria, producing 48,562 unique criteria in total. OpenAI reports that its model o3 outperforms other models including Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro, and that its frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench in recent months, a larger improvement than between GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 Turbo. The benchmark also shows that small models have improved substantially, with GPT-4.1 nano outperforming August 2024's GPT-4o despite being 25 times cheaper, a finding with direct implications for deployment in low-resource settings. HealthBench Hard, a subset of 1,000 examples that today's frontier models still struggle with, signals that significant gaps in clinical reasoning remain.

On the vendor side, KLAS Research provides what it describes as candid provider feedback from executives, physicians, nurses, IT professionals, and administrators, rating healthcare IT vendors on real-world experience rather than vendor claims, and has done so since 1996. Its annual Best in KLAS report ranks vendors against provider and payer feedback gathered throughout the year. Independently, Artificial Analysis publishes vendor-neutral comparisons of models on performance metrics including quality, price, output speed, and latency, covering providers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral, and others, giving procurement teams a second layer of benchmarking that is not sourced from the vendors themselves. Rock Health tracks the capital flowing into digital health and clinical AI, and its funding research is widely cited as the standard record of where venture money is landing in the sector, though the specific figures from its most recent reporting are not reproduced in the source material available here.

The WHO's guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health is the reference document that member-state health systems are expected to work from. Produced after eighteen months of deliberation among experts in ethics, digital technology, law, and human rights alongside ministry of health officials, it identifies ethical challenges and risks in clinical AI deployment and establishes six consensus principles intended to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries. The WHO report explicitly calls for putting ethics and human rights at the heart of design, deployment, and use, and for holding both public and private sector stakeholders accountable to healthcare workers and the communities affected. That governance frame matters practically because organizations deploying clinical AI in international or cross-border contexts will find regulators referencing WHO principles, and domestic regulators in many countries are aligning their guidance to it.

For an organization deciding whether to deploy, the headline Census figure of 23.5% adoption means a meaningful share of the sector is already using AI but a larger share is not, so first-mover pressure is real without being overwhelming. The existence of HealthBench and KLAS ratings means there are now external, physician-grounded, and provider-experienced standards against which to evaluate vendor claims rather than accepting them at face value. The NIH's emphasis on FAIR data and the WHO's governance principles together indicate that data quality, interoperability, and documented ethical review are prerequisites rather than optional considerations, and organizations that have not addressed those foundations will find them the binding constraint on any clinical AI deployment.
